parsedVerdict.reasoning:
PlaceOrderUseCase.execute does application-layer work. It checks the input (customerId and items), loads products through the domain's ProductRepository port, and calls the domain method product.reserve. It builds the Order aggregate, saves it through the OrderRepository port, and maps the result to a CreateOrderResponse in toResponse. The file contains no transport, framework, HTTP or concrete persistence code. The repository interfaces are injected, not implemented here.

Two checks are borderline. 'Order must contain at least one item' and the stock comparison (product.getStock() < item.quantity) could arguably be enforced inside the Order and Product domain classes. Even so, checking every item before reserving any stock is a legitimate application concern: it stops some products from being reserved when a later item fails. These checks also rely on domain queries instead of restating domain calculations.

The use case does not take over core domain behaviour; reservation is still done by Product.reserve. Building the ID with Date.now() and mapping to the DTO are also acceptable here. Overall the file matches the application layer's role.
